source_user: Explain how speculative decoding interacts with latency, throughput, or memory. Case variant 3: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Speculative decoding uses a draft model to propose tokens and a target model to verify them; speedup depends on acceptance rate and verification cost.
corrected_answer:
How speculative decoding trades latency, throughput, and memory.

Scope and assumptions (state these before any number is quoted): single-node GPU serving, continuous batching, draft and target models share a tokenizer and vocabulary, and verification uses the standard rejection-sampling rule so the output distribution is provably identical to plain target-model sampling. Every threshold below is a measurement target, not a constant.

Concrete mechanism. In the memory-bound decode regime, one target forward step costs roughly t_step ~= model_bytes_read / effective_HBM_bandwidth, and that cost is almost independent of how many tokens are scored in the step, because the same weights are streamed once. Speculative decoding exploits exactly this: a cheap draft proposes gamma tokens, the target verifies all gamma+1 positions in a single batched forward, and the accepted prefix is emitted. If the expected number of accepted tokens per target step is E[a], the wall-clock speedup is approximately E[a] / (1 + gamma * c_draft/c_target), where c_draft/c_target is the per-step cost ratio. This is why draft cost, not just acceptance rate, decides the outcome.

Latency. Interactive TPOT is where the technique is designed to win, because small-batch decode leaves HBM bandwidth partly idle and speculation converts idle bandwidth into emitted tokens. Expect the win to show up as reduced median and p90 inter-token latency, but note that speculation makes per-step token yield stochastic, so p99 TPOT can widen even when the median improves. Report the full distribution, never just the mean.

Throughput. Throughput gains are not guaranteed and often invert at high load. Once the target model is already running at a large effective batch, the verification forward is compute-bound, and the extra gamma positions per sequence consume FLOPs that would otherwise have served other requests. Rejected drafts are pure waste. At high concurrency, speculative decoding can reduce aggregate tokens/sec while still improving single-stream latency.

Memory. Two costs. First, the draft model's weights are resident alongside the target, reducing the KV-cache budget and therefore the maximum concurrency. Second, verification must maintain KV state for speculated positions and roll back the rejected suffix; implementations either over-allocate gamma extra KV slots per in-flight sequence or pay a copy on rollback. With paged KV, the block allocator must handle partial-block truncation cleanly.

Boundary condition. The technique stops paying off once the decode step is no longer memory-bound, i.e. once batch size times speculation width pushes the verification GEMM into the compute-bound region. Equivalently, if E[a] <= 1 + gamma * c_draft/c_target, speculation is a net loss. A short, badly-aligned draft on out-of-distribution traffic (code, other languages, long-context tails) can push acceptance low enough to cross that line even though a benchmark on in-distribution prompts looked good.

Falsifiable hypothesis. "Enabling speculative decoding with this draft at gamma=4 reduces p90 TPOT by at least 25 percent at our production concurrency without reducing tokens/sec by more than 5 percent."

Evidence required. Measured acceptance-rate distribution per traffic segment, per-step draft and target latency, TTFT/TPOT/p99 under the real arrival process, tokens/sec at fixed concurrency with and without speculation, KV-cache occupancy and admitted-concurrency delta, and an output-equivalence test showing identical distributions under a fixed seed.

Rollback threshold. Revert if p99 TPOT regresses, if throughput at peak concurrency drops beyond the agreed budget, if acceptance rate on any significant traffic segment falls below the break-even point, or if output-equivalence checks fail. Ship behind a per-route flag with adaptive gamma so speculation can be disabled under load without a redeploy.

omission invites the reader to assume speculative decoding is a universal speedup, which is false at high concurrency
no memory accounting for draft weights and speculated KV slots, so a capacity regression could ship unnoticed
no output-equivalence check mentioned, so a lossy acceptance rule could be mistaken for a free speedup

measured draft and target per-step latency to compute c_draft/c_target and the break-even point

source_user: Give a measurement plan for validating whether speculative decoding helps a serving workload. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Speculative decoding uses a draft model to propose tokens and a target model to verify them; speedup depends on acceptance rate and verification cost.
corrected_answer:
Measurement plan: does speculative decoding actually help this serving workload?

Framing. The claim under test is a per-workload claim, not a property of the technique. The plan must be able to return "no", so define the failure condition before collecting data.

Hypothesis. "For our production traffic mix, draft D at speculation width gamma reduces p90 time-per-output-token by at least X percent at our target concurrency, without reducing peak tokens/sec by more than Y percent, and without changing output distribution."

Step 1: fix the baseline. Pin engine version, model weights, quantization, batching policy, KV block size, and GPU clocks (lock clocks or record them; thermal drift silently invalidates A/B runs). Record the baseline TTFT, TPOT, p50/p90/p99, tokens/sec, and KV occupancy.

Step 2: characterize the traffic, not a benchmark. Replay real prompt and output-length distributions per segment (chat, code, summarization, long-context, non-English). Acceptance rate is highly segment-dependent, and an aggregate mean will hide a segment where speculation is a net loss.

Step 3: instrument the mechanism directly. Log per target step: number of proposed tokens, number accepted, draft forward latency, target verification latency. From these derive the empirical acceptance distribution and the break-even inequality E[a] > 1 + gamma * c_draft/c_target. This is the concrete mechanism the whole decision rests on; without per-step acceptance logging you are guessing.

Step 4: sweep, do not spot-check. Vary gamma over a range (for example 1 to 8) crossed with concurrency from single-stream to saturation. Report a surface, because the sign of the effect flips across it: latency wins concentrate at low concurrency, throughput losses concentrate at saturation.

Step 5: load model. Use an open-loop generator at fixed arrival rate rather than a closed-loop fixed-concurrency client. Closed-loop harnesses mask queueing collapse and will overstate the benefit.

Step 6: correctness gate. Verify output equivalence: with a fixed seed and the rejection-sampling rule, speculative output must match non-speculative output. Any mismatch means a sampler or rollback bug, and all performance numbers are void until it is fixed.

Step 7: statistics. Minimum three interleaved A/B repetitions per cell, report confidence intervals, and discard the first warmup window (CUDA graph capture, allocator warmup, and cache fill make early samples unrepresentative).

Boundary condition. The plan is only valid while decode is memory-bound. Once batch times gamma pushes verification into the compute-bound regime, extra speculated positions steal FLOPs from other requests, so the measured throughput delta must be collected at real peak load, not at a comfortable operating point.

Decision rule. Adopt only if the latency target is met at production concurrency AND throughput loss is within budget AND every traffic segment is above break-even AND output equivalence passes. Otherwise adopt narrowly, gated per route, with adaptive gamma that falls back to gamma=0 under queue pressure.

Rollback threshold. Any p99 TPOT regression, any throughput loss beyond budget at peak, or any equivalence failure triggers immediate disable via the flag.
